title: Numeric Data Types
description: Master SMALLINT, INTEGER, BIGINT, NUMERIC/DECIMAL, REAL, and DOUBLE PRECISION for scientific and financial accuracy.

data.text: Choosing the appropriate numeric type affects both physical storage footprint and calculation precision. PostgreSQL offers integer types for counting, arbitrary-precision decimals for currency, and floating-point types for scientific computation.

rows: Small enum codes, status flags, days of week
Large table primary keys, financial micro-units
Up to 131,072 digits before decimal; 16,383 digits after
Financial balances, money, invoices (zero rounding error)
Scientific measurements where rounding is acceptable

data.text: Integers are exact and fast. The only real decision is how big they need to be. A `SMALLINT` column that later hits 32,767 rows is a production incident, so the safe default for identifiers is `BIGINT` — 8 bytes is cheap, and running out of `INTEGER` range on a busy table is not.

data.title: Integer Arithmetic, Overflow, and Casting
data.content: PostgreSQL raises an error on overflow rather than silently wrapping.
data.code:
SELECT 2147483647::int + 1;
-- ERROR:  integer out of range

SELECT (2147483647::int + 1)::bigint;   -- correct: widen before adding

-- Division of integers truncates: watch out in averages
SELECT 7 / 2 AS integer_division,          -- 3
       7::numeric / 2 AS exact_division;    -- 3.5

-- Rounding helpers
SELECT round(2.5::numeric, 0) AS half_up,   -- 3 (numeric rounds half away from zero)
       trunc(2.9)             AS truncated; -- 2

-- Casting text to integer is strict: '12abc' raises an error
SELECT '12abc'::integer;                    -- ERROR: invalid input syntax

data.text: Binary floating point cannot represent 0.1 exactly. Sum enough of them and the error becomes visible — the classic `0.1 + 0.2 = 0.30000000000000004` problem. `NUMERIC(p, s)` stores a scaled integer with an exact decimal scale, so currency arithmetic is exact.

data.title: The Float Trap and the Numeric Fix
data.content: A one-cent discrepancy in a payments table is a bug report.
data.code:
-- Float accumulates error
SELECT 0.1::float8 + 0.2::float8 = 0.3::float8;   -- false

-- NUMERIC is exact
SELECT 0.1::numeric + 0.2::numeric = 0.3::numeric; -- true

CREATE TABLE invoices (
    id       BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
    amount   NUMERIC(12, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (amount >= 0),   -- max 9,999,999,999.99
    tax_rate NUMERIC(5, 4)  NOT NULL DEFAULT 0.2000
);

INSERT INTO invoices (amount) VALUES (19.99), (5.01);
SELECT sum(amount) AS exact_total FROM invoices;   -- 25.00

-- NUMERIC division: set the scale explicitly
SELECT round(19.99::numeric * 0.20, 2) AS tax;      -- 4.00

data.title: Interview Answer
data.text: The expected answer to "which numeric type would you use for money?" is `NUMERIC` (alias `DECIMAL`), because binary floating point cannot represent decimal fractions exactly. Add that `NUMERIC` is slower than `BIGINT`, so some teams store **integer minor units** (cents) instead — both are correct, and naming the trade-off is what earns the point.

data.title: Prove the Float Problem
data.description: Demonstrate floating-point error and fix it.
steps: Insert 100 rows of `0.1::real` into a table and sum them.
Explain in one sentence why the values differ.
Design an `accounts` table with a `balance NUMERIC(14,2)` and a `CHECK (balance >= 0)` constraint.
data.expectedOutcome: You can reproduce and explain binary floating-point rounding on demand.

items.question: Is `INTEGER` faster than `BIGINT`?
items.answer: Marginally: 4 vs 8 bytes affects cache density and index size, but on modern hardware that rarely justifies the risk of overflow. Use `BIGINT` for identifiers and `INTEGER`/`SMALLINT` for small enumerated values.

items.question: What is `MONEY` and why is it discouraged?
items.answer: A built-in type with locale-dependent formatting and fixed scale of 4. It is tied to `lc_monetary`, which makes it fragile across environments; `NUMERIC(12,2)` is more portable and explicit.

items.question: Does `NUMERIC` waste storage?
items.answer: It uses a variable-length decimal representation, roughly 4 bytes per 4 digits plus overhead. It is more expensive than `BIGINT` but exact — use it where exactness is required.

data.title: Key Takeaways
points: Use `BIGINT GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY` for primary keys; `SMALLINT` only for small, bounded code values.
`NUMERIC`/`DECIMAL` is exact and is the correct choice for money; floating point is not.
Integer division truncates — cast to `NUMERIC` before dividing when you need a fraction.
PostgreSQL errors on integer overflow rather than silently wrapping.
data.takeaway: Money → `NUMERIC`. IDs → `BIGINT`. Science → `DOUBLE PRECISION`. That is the whole interview answer.
